subtype: Pressure to protect the institution's name [Receiver]
passage:
Dear Yamini,
You asked me to tell you how it went. I reported a senior who kept sending me messages after I asked him to stop. On Monday the head of department called me in and said, “A complaint like this will damage the college’s name, and the accreditation visit is next month. Are you sure?”
I went home feeling guilty and afraid. I typed a withdrawal note twice and deleted it.
This afternoon I took the message to Dr. Rao, the ombuds officer. She said the complaint was mine to keep and that the college’s name was not mine to guard. She opened the file that same day and introduced me to the counsellor.
I haven’t withdrawn.
Vinita

qa.q: Who did Vinita take the head of department's message to?
qa.a: Vinita took it to Dr. Rao, the ombuds officer.

qa.q: Why did Vinita type a withdrawal note twice?
qa.a: Vinita felt guilty and afraid after being told the complaint could damage the college's name. The pressure made giving up feel like an escape.

qa.q: What did Dr. Rao do that made a difference?
qa.a: Dr. Rao said the complaint was Vinita's to keep, that the college's name was not Vinita's to guard, and opened the file that same day. Vinita was also introduced to the counsellor.

qa.q: How might the head of department see the situation differently from Vinita?
qa.a: The head of department may be worried about the accreditation visit and the college's reputation. Those worries are real but should not outweigh Vinita's report.

grounding: Shows a student who reports harassment being told it will damage the college's name, feeling guilt and fear, and getting support.

Irfan, you asked what it was like. I’m Dilnaz, and last term I reported a copying ring in our department. Two days later the assistant registrar called me in. “Think of the college’s ranking,” they said. “One story like this and admissions drop. Wouldn’t it be kinder to let it go?”
That night I filled in the withdrawal form. I sat with the pen above the line. In class someone whispered, “You’ll ruin us all.”
You sat beside me in the canteen the next day, and I told you. That afternoon I met the student ombuds officer, who said reporting cheating wasn’t my fault and forwarded my report to the committee.
I still haven’t signed the form.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz report last term?
qa.a: Dilnaz reported a copying ring in the department.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling when the pen hovered above the line on the withdrawal form?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt guilty and frightened, and wanted the pressure to stop. Being told it could hurt the college and hearing the whisper about ruining everyone made giving up tempting.

qa.q: What helped Dilnaz stay with the complaint?
qa.a: Dilnaz told Irfan, and the student ombuds officer that same afternoon said it wasn't Dilnaz's fault and passed the report on. Support turned pressure into something Dilnaz did not face alone.

qa.q: How might the assistant registrar have seen the situation?
qa.a: They may have been worried about the college's ranking and admissions. Their words, one story and admissions drop, show a concern for the institution over the report.

grounding: Shows a student reporting cheating and pressured to protect the college's name, almost withdrawing and then getting support.
